newsitem.title: UK: RUGBY UNION-SELLA ADVISES FRENCH TO STRIKE QUICKLY.
newsitem.headline: RUGBY UNION-SELLA ADVISES FRENCH TO STRIKE QUICKLY.

text.p: France must aim to reproduce the sort of early masterpiece which dazzled Twickenham six years ago if they want to stop England entering the Five Nations 'Hall of Fame' next month.
That is the view of the world's most-capped player Philippe Sella who has enjoyed a first-hand view of the improvements in English rugby since his arrival in London to play club rugby with Saracens.
It is a decade since France won at Twickenham and, should they be planning a waiting game in Saturday's crunch encounter, Sella fears they will again return home disappointed.

The former French centre has been as impressed as anyone by the way England dismantled Scotland and Ireland in record style in the closing stages of their opening games and believes how his country cope early on will determine the outcome.
"For the French team it is very important to be stronger than Ireland or Scotland for the first hour. The truth is the key to the game will be the first half," Sella said on Wednesday.
"If the initial pressure is exerted by England it will be very difficult. They have played strong rugby for the first hour in both their games and have been very good in the last 20 minutes."

Sella was personally involved in Twickenham's "Try of the Century' scored by Philippe Saint-Andre in the initial stages of the 1991 encounter between the two sides, although England still won 21-19 to seal the first of two successive grand slams.

He also grabbed the vital interception try which secured a 19-15 win for France in 1987, the last time 'Les Bleus' defeated the English on home soil, and is keen for the current side to rise to the big Twickenham occasion against a team bidding for a record third successive outright Five Nations title.

"It is difficult at Twickenham and France's record there has been very disappointing, but it's also a great place to play," said Sella, scheduled to grace the arena again when he captains a World XV against the English club champions in May.

"Both teams are unbeaten and it's basically a final. The French will want to play a lot of running rugby but it's very important they keep hold of the ball. Against Wales they showed a lot of moves, but they must do the simple things well too.

"I think England have shown more confidence in the opening two games, they've looked very strong. The bookmakers think they are favourites, but in sport one can't always say that one team is going to win."

Sella faced England 15 times in a career which brought him 111 caps for his country, winning on six occasions, but the former Agen player has been enthusiastically welcomed since transferring to English club rugby.
"When we signed him people said he was over the hill. If that's so he must have been a hell of a player in his prime." said Saracens coach Mark Evans last month.
In turn, the French contingent have been impressed with what they have found, notably former Racing Club flanker Laurent Cabannes, now at Harlequins.
"Some referees blow up for incredible things and there's never a word," he said. "The English players never argue. It's quite unique; their approach to discipline is an example."

Visitors to Twickenham this weekend may even spot Laurent Benezech's face plastered across the side of a bus advertising Harlequins' ground across from the main stadium, and Sella confirms more French players "are in contact with English clubs".

Several British clubs, particularly in Wales, are nevertheless struggling to pay the inflated wages they offered players at the start of the season, and Va'aiga Tuigamala's million-pound transfer to Newcastle last week has been greeted with a mixture of envy and scorn.

Scotland and Ireland, despite agreeing a three-year contract to keep their home matches on terrestrial television for the next three years, are among those engaged in a bitter fight to keep their best players at home.

Almost half the players involved in Saturday's other international at Murrayfield play their club rugby in England, but can expect a share of the Five Nations wooden spoon if they fail to finish on the winning side. Scotland have won eight and drawn one of the last nine meetings. France beating England at Twickenham is like discovering coq au vin as the dish of the day at a British motorway cafe -- it doesn't happen often.
It is 10 years since France triumphed It's been a pleasure for me and my family to be here.
